The environment includes protein-like concentrationdynamics, membrane integrity, abstract functional role coverage, and division-like events, whileexpressivity is varied through three regimes controlling coupling strength, feedback structure, and internalmemory. Performance is evaluated using survival rate, success rate, mean functional role coverage, andmean number of division events. Across regimes, survival reached 100%, but success increased from 67.5%in the low-expressivity regime to 97.5% in the mid regime and 100% in the high regime. The findingsposition maximum-entropy reinforcement learning as a diagnostic tool for identifying missing structuralingredients in computational origin-of-life models.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.31449/inf.v50i14.13944\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 8, 6]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4680117\", \"title\": [\"A Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning-Aware Hyper-Heuristic Algorithm with Fitness Landscape Analysis\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4680117\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7669903\", \"title\": [\"Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Factorized State Spaces: Coordination without Full-State Sharing\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The parallel loop architecture of the cortico-basal ganglia system suggests that coordination of multiple reinforcement learning modules with different state and action spaces allows flexible and robust learning and control. Many previous hierarchical reinforcement learning approaches assumed that modules at different hierarchical levels access the same observation space with different spatial or temporal scales. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical reinforcement learning architecture where each level works in a distinct subspace of the entire state space. We first formulate the hierarchically decomposable Markov decision process (HDMDP), in which environmental dynamics are factorized into high- and low-level components, with low-level state transitions producing abstract effects that condition high-level transitions. We then propose hierarchically decomposed reinforcement learning (HDRL) in which the high-level module observes only the high-level state and selects a command corresponding to a desired high-level state transition, whereas the low-level module observes only the low-level state and the command from the high-level to select a primitive action. To address the partial observability in the high-level, we introduce command relabeling based on realized high-level transitions and infeasible command pruning to remove commands that are infeasible. Experiments on a discrete Grid Walk task with low-level locomotion dynamics showed that HDRL can learn the task more efficiently than flat Q-learning using full-state observations. Ablations showed that pruning accelerated learning but sometimes reduced stability, whereas combining pruning with relabeling was most stable. Experiments on a continuous Cart-Pole Navigation task showed that only variants with relabeling succeeded. Although there are numerous hippocampal modeling approaches, only a few span the wide functionalities ranging from processing raw sensory signals to planning and action generation. This paper presents a vision-based navigation system that involves generating place and HD cells through learning from visual images, building topological maps based on learned cell representations and performing navigation using hierarchical reinforcement learning. First, place and HD cells are trained from sequences of visual stimuli in an unsupervised learning fashion. A modified Slow Feature Analysis (SFA) algorithm is proposed to learn different cell types in an intentional way by restricting their learning to separate phases of the spatial exploration. Then, to extract the encoded metric information from these unsupervised learning representations, a self-organized learning algorithm is adopted to learn over the emerged cell activities and to generate topological maps that reveal the topology of the environment and information about a robot’s head direction, respectively. This enables the robot to perform self-localization and orientation detection based on the generated maps. Finally, goal-directed navigation is performed using reinforcement learning in continuous state spaces which are represented by the population activities of place cells. In particular, considering that the topological map provides a natural hierarchical representation of the environment, hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) is used to exploit this hierarchy to accelerate learning. The HRL works on different spatial scales, where a high-level policy learns to select subgoals and a low-level policy learns over primitive actions to specialize on the selected subgoals.
